title: Density-wave order enhances the phonon thermal Hall effect in a trilayer nickelate
authors: Qiaochao Xiang, Enkang Zhang, Xiaokang Li, Xiaodong Guo, Mengfei Zhu, Jun Zhao, Guang-Ming Zhang, Liang Li, Zengwei Zhu
abstract: Ruddlesden--Popper nickelates have emerged as a promising platform for high-temperature superconductivity, yet the role of lattice degrees of freedom in their correlated normal state remains largely unexplored. Here, we report the observation of a finite phonon thermal Hall effect in the trilayer nickelate La$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$ at ambient pressure. Remarkably, the thermal Hall response is strongly enhanced below the density-wave transition at $T^*\approx140$ K, exhibiting two distinct plateaus in the thermal Hall resistivity. The characteristic energy scale extracted from the thermal Hall response ($\sim4.1$ meV) closely matches the magnon--phonon crossing span energy ($\sim3.2$ meV), pointing to magnon--phonon hybridization as the primary mechanism enhancing the thermal Hall effect. These results provide new insight into the interplay between lattice and spin excitations in nickelates, with implications for understanding both their superconductivity and the multiple possible origins of insulating thermal Hall signals.
summary: The authors report observing a large, enhanced phonon thermal Hall effect in the nickelate $	ext{La}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$ below its density-wave transition temperature. By measuring multiple transport properties and ruling out electronic or simple phonon-drag contributions, they attribute the signal to magnon-phonon hybridization driven by spin-lattice coupling. This reveals a crucial interplay between magnetic order and lattice dynamics in these superconducting materials.
main_problem: The study investigates the role of lattice degrees of freedom in the normal state of Ruddlesden–Popper nickelates, specifically focusing on the origin and enhancement mechanism of the phonon thermal Hall effect.
main_result: The enhanced transverse thermal conductivity ($\kappa_{xy}$) below the density-wave transition is strongly attributed to phonons coupled via magnon-phonon hybridization driven by spin-lattice coupling. This signal significantly exceeds contributions from electronic carriers or simple phonon drag mechanisms.
method: The research employs transport measurements, measuring longitudinal and transverse thermal conductivities ($\kappa_{xx}, \kappa_{xy}$), magnetoresistance, and Seebeck/Nernst coefficients as a function of temperature and magnetic field.
model_or_system: The physical system is the trilayer nickelate $	ext{La}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$, which exhibits density-wave order. The underlying physics involves charge-lattice coupling, where hybridization between apical oxygen $2p$ and Ni $3d_{z^2}$ orbitals creates local dipoles that interact with magnetic fields.

main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the electronic contribution can be estimated via the Wiedemann–Franz law, and it estimates an upper bound for phonon-drag using $S_{xx}T\alpha_{xy}$.
figures_summary: Figures show $\kappa_{xy}$ enhancement below $T^*$, confirming phononic origin over electronic contributions. They also compare measured $\kappa_{xy}$ against the calculated phonon-drag limit, showing a large discrepancy.
paper_structure: The paper systematically measures various transport coefficients ($ho, \kappa, S, \alpha$) under varying magnetic fields and temperatures to isolate the source of transverse heat transport, culminating in a comparison that rules out simple models like phonon drag.
why_interesting: This work provides experimental evidence for how electronic order (density waves) can couple strongly to lattice vibrations (phonons), leading to exotic thermal responses. This coupling mechanism is relevant to understanding emergent quantum phenomena in correlated materials.
